The intuition is that when the generated samples have disjoint support from the data, the generated distribution at the data support may not be updated using standard training. This is exactly one source of mode collapse.

In our proposed training method, when $x=1$, the optimal update direction is given by~[REF:eq:update_pg], where $\tilde{p}_g$ is a large value because $D(1) = 1$. Therefore, by [REF:eq:update_gen], the second term in the loss function is very large, which forces the generator to generate samples at $G(\bz) = 1$.
The primal-dual update rules will guarantee convergence of $\left( \bD^{(t)}, \bp_g^{(t)} \right)$ to the primal-dual saddle point ($\bD^{\ast},\bp^{\ast}_g$).

paper.title: Local Convergence of Gradient Descent-Ascent for Training Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a popular formulation to train generative models for complex high dimensional data. The standard method for training GANs involves a gradient descent-ascent (GDA) procedure on a minimax optimization problem. This procedure is hard to analyze in general due to the nonlinear nature of the dynamics. We study the local dynamics of GDA for training a GAN with a kernel-based discriminator. This convergence analysis is based on a linearization of a non-linear dynamical system that describes the GDA iterations, under an \textit{isolated points model} assumption from [Becker et al. 2022]. Our analysis brings out the effect of the learning rates, regularization, and the bandwidth of the kernel discriminator, on the local convergence rate of GDA. Importantly, we show phase transitions that indicate when the system converges, oscillates, or diverges. We also provide numerical simulations that verify our claims.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper analyzes the coupled generator/discriminator GDA dynamics for a kernel-based (RBF/MMD) discriminator GAN under an isolated-points model. It linearizes the joint update map around the equilibrium where generated points sit on true points and derives an exact eigenvalue characterization in terms of the generator and discriminator learning rates (and their ratio μ), regularization λ, and kernel width σ, giving necessary/sufficient conditions for local stability, convergence-rate bounds, and phase transitions between convergence, oscillation, and divergence. This bears on the synchronization problem by quantifying how mismatched generator-vs-discriminator learning (e.g., too-large η_g relative to η_d and kernel capacity) destabilizes training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's core problem is mode collapse / the 'Helvetica scenario': if G is trained too much without D being kept synchronized, many z values collapse to the same x and diversity is lost. The paper does not analyze this scenario: its local analysis is confined to neighborhoods of an equilibrium where generated points already match the true points, under strong assumptions (isolated points, RBF kernel with zero cross-region interaction, equal generated masses), and it studies whether points converge to the true samples, not whether the generator's latent diversity collapses into a single mode or which z-values map to the same output. It never models an over-trained generator versus a stale/under-trained discriminator, and it provides no synchronization scheduling rule (e.g., number/ratio of D updates per G update) to prevent mode collapse. Its contribution is instead stability and convergence-rate conditions for simultaneous GDA around an equilibrium, which is only tangentially related to keeping D synchronized to avoid diversity collapse.
evidence_snippets: Our analysis brings out the effect of the learning rates, regularization, and the bandwidth of the kernel discriminator, on the local convergence rate of GDA. Importantly, we show phase transitions that indicate when the system converges, oscillates, or diverges.

In practice, however, we apply GDA for training GANs, whereby the discriminator is not allowed to converge, making analysis of the iterative training extremely difficult. Furthermore, training commonly suffers from empirical breakdowns such as mode collapse, in which the entire generated distribution converges to a small portion of the target distribution
The training dynamics [REF:eq:gda_local] are stable around equilibrium $\wt\X_i^*$ from [REF:eq:xeq] for all $\Delta_i \in (0,p_i)$ if, ... $\eta_d < \frac2\lambda$, and $\eta_g<\lambda\sigma^2$.

paper.title: Interaction Matters: A Note on Non-asymptotic Local Convergence of Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Motivated by the pursuit of a systematic computational and algorithmic understanding of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we present a simple yet unified non-asymptotic local convergence theory for smooth two-player games, which subsumes several discrete-time gradient-based saddle point dynamics. The analysis reveals the surprising nature of the off-diagonal interaction term as both a blessing and a curse. On the one hand, this interaction term explains the origin of the slow-down effect in the convergence of Simultaneous Gradient Ascent (SGA) to stable Nash equilibria. On the other hand, for the unstable equilibria, exponential convergence can be proved thanks to the interaction term, for four modified dynamics proposed to stabilize GAN training: Optimistic Mirror Descent (OMD), Consensus Optimization (CO), Implicit Updates (IU) and Predictive Method (PM). The analysis uncovers the intimate connections among these stabilizing techniques, and provides detailed characterization on the choice of learning rate. As a by-product, we present a new analysis for OMD proposed in Daskalakis, Ilyas, Syrgkanis, and Zeng [2017] with improved rates.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper develops a non-asymptotic local convergence theory for discrete-time gradient-based dynamics (SGA, OMD, Consensus Optimization, Implicit Updates, Predictive Methods) on smooth two-player zero-sum games of GAN form. It characterizes exponential convergence to stable local Nash equilibria for SGA and exponential convergence to unstable (bi-linear) equilibria for the four modified dynamics, framing the off-diagonal interaction term as both a curse and a blessing for convergence rates. These results concern which update *dynamics* converge and at what rate, under the assumption that both players are updated simultaneously (once per iteration).
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem is that the discriminator and generator must remain synchronized in update frequency — training G too much without updating D causes the "Helvetica scenario" in which many z collapse to the same x (mode collapse). This paper never studies imbalanced/asymmetric update schedules between the two players: all analyzed dynamics (SGA, OMD, CO, IU, PM) and all experiments update generator and discriminator together once per iteration. It does not analyze regimes where one player is updated more often than the other, does not discuss the k-D-steps-per-G-step rule, and does not connect unequal update rates to diversity loss/mode collapse or the Helvetica scenario. Its scope is instead local convergence rates of equal-rate simultaneous dynamics toward local Nash equilibria, so the synchronization problem motivating the gap remains open.
evidence_snippets: The simplest possibility is Simultaneous Gradient Ascent (SGA), which corresponds to the following discrete-time dynamical system, ...
In this section we will establish the non-asymptotic convergence of SGA dynamics to saddle points that are stable local Nash equilibria.
we optimize the above loss functions using simultaneous gradient updates with fixed learning rate of $\eta = 10^{-3}$.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: This is a focused, empirically testable extension of existing GAN work. The needed data is cheap and standard (toy Gaussian mixtures for controlled mode-collapse measurement, plus MNIST/CIFAR if desired), and compute is modest — varying the G:D update ratio requires only small-scale GAN training runs on a single GPU. The methodological path is a direct extension of known training loops: sweep update-count/learning-rate ratios, intentionally stale the discriminator, and measure mode collapse with established diversity metrics (number of recovered modes, precision/recall, FID). The main feasibility risks are GAN training variance and the need for careful seeds/repeats, but these are manageable engineering concerns, not fundamental barriers; a clear empirical answer (and possibly a simple scheduling rule) is achievable.

ranked.title: Parzen window likelihood estimate unreliable in high dimensions
ranked.description: The Gaussian Parzen window method used to estimate test likelihood has somewhat high variance and does not perform well in high-dimensional spaces, though the authors state it is the best method available to their knowledge.
ranked.canonical_description: Parzen window likelihood estimate has high variance and fails in high dimensions

evidence.anchor: estimating the likelihood has somewhat high variance
evidence.quote: This method of estimating the likelihood has somewhat high variance

verdict.reasoning: The gap's specific problem — the Gaussian Parzen window estimator of test likelihood having high variance and failing in high dimensions — is not directly fixed by any paper, but several papers make genuine partial progress on the underlying difficulty. The SVS estimator (Paper 1) attacks the variance side of high-dimensional kernel density estimation and shows MISE/ISE gains at d=10, but only under a sparse active-set structure and without evaluating test-likelihood estimates or their variance at held-out points. The simplified vine copula KDE (Paper 2) proves a dimension-independent convergence rate, but this requires the true density to be a simplified vine distribution and again does not address Parzen-window test-likelihood reliability. The adaptive hyperbolic cross estimator (Paper 5) provides nearly dimension-free IPM rates under mixed smooth Sobolev structure, but replaces the kernel estimator rather than improving it and does not treat pointwise test-likelihood variance. Papers 3 and 4 are not addressed: they study Markov-structured histogram estimation and tensorizing flow, respectively, without engaging Parzen-window likelihood estimation. So the high-dimensional density-estimation curse has been partially circumvented through structurally constrained alternative estimators, but the specific task named in the gap — reliable Gaussian Parzen-window test-likelihood estimation in high dimensions — remains open, keeping this from being solved.

paper.title: Sparse Variable Sharpening in High-Dimensional Kernel Density Estimation
paper.abstract: High-dimensional kernel density estimation suffers from the curse of dimensionality. This study proposes a hybrid density estimator defined as the product of a joint density over a pre-specified subset of dimensions and marginal densities for the remaining variables, instead of estimating the full high-dimensional density directly. Under this framework, given the observed data, we select a subset of variables for joint density construction to improve estimation accuracy, while modeling the remaining variables through their respective marginal densities. This construction involves a trade-off between the approximation error induced by simplifying the dependence structure and the variance reduction achieved by lowering the dimension of the joint density. We employ a genetic algorithm to efficiently identify such variable subsets. Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate that the proposed estimator can outperform conventional full-dimensional kernel density estimation when this trade-off is appropriately balanced.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper targets the high-variance/failure of kernel (Parzen-window-type) density estimators in high dimensions. It proposes a "sparse variable-sharpening" KDE (SVS) that avoids a full d-dimensional joint estimate: it estimates a joint density only over a selected active variable subset (with sharpening exponents) and multiplies in marginal KDEs for the rest. The paper derives the bias, variance, MISE rate O(N^{-4/(|S|+4)} + |\bar{S}|N^{-4/5}) + approximation error, and asymptotic normality, and validates via oracle calibration plus Monte-Carlo simulations at d=10 showing SVS can beat the full-joint KDE (and sometimes PPDE) in ISE — i.e., it attacks the variance side of the stated problem.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is specifically about the reliability/variance of Parzen-window estimates of *test likelihood* in high-dimensional settings (the kind of usage where the Parzen estimate is claimed to be the best available). The paper does not evaluate likelihood estimates at held-out test points or their variance at all — its evidence is MISE/ISE over the full density. Its gains are demonstrated only for d=10 and rely on sparsity structure: for Type J1 the truth has a low-dimensional active set, and for Type AR1 the method explicitly trades a nonzero approximation error for variance reduction at small N; for general high-dimensional densities without a small active subset, SVS is not consistent and inherits the same high-dimensional difficulty. Tuning remains heuristic (b = d or b = d/2 two-mode scheme). Thus it offers a variance-reduced KDE variant relevant to the underlying problem but does not resolve the stated problem of reliable Parzen-window test-likelihood estimation in high dimensions.
evidence_snippets: In particular, the impact of dimensionality arises primarily from the variance term, whose order deteriorates exponentially with the dimension, whereas the bias term does not explicitly depend on the dimension for a fixed bandwidth.

The advantage of this approach is that, instead of estimating a full $d$-dimensional KDE, we only need to estimate $|S|$-dimensional KDE together with $d-|S|$ one-dimensional KDEs. As a result, when the sample size is insufficient for reliable full-dimensional estimation, this method may yield a more accurate approximation than the standard $d$-dimensional KDE.

Thus, SVS consistently reduces the estimation error relative to the full-joint KDE under the AR1 setting, indicating that the variance reduction achieved through the sparse representation can remain beneficial even when the sparse approximation does not fully capture the true density and hence incurs a nonzero approximation error.

paper.title: Evading the curse of dimensionality in nonparametric density estimation with simplified vine copulas
paper.abstract: Practical applications of nonparametric density estimators in more than three dimensions suffer a great deal from the well-known curse of dimensionality: convergence slows down as dimension increases. We show that one can evade the curse of dimensionality by assuming a simplified vine copula model for the dependence between variables. We formulate a general nonparametric estimator for such a model and show under high-level assumptions that the speed of convergence is independent of dimension. We further discuss a particular implementation for which we validate the high-level assumptions and establish its asymptotic normality. Simulation experiments illustrate a large gain in finite sample performance when the simplifying assumption is at least approximately true. But even when it is severely violated, the vine copula based approach proves advantageous as soon as more than a few variables are involved. Lastly, we give an application of the estimator to a classification problem from astrophysics.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper tackles the root cause of the gap — the curse of dimensionality that makes nonparametric (kernel/Parzen-type) density estimation unreliable in high dimensions. It proposes a nonparametric density estimator based on simplified vine copulas that decomposes the d-dimensional estimation problem into univariate marginal and bivariate pair-copula estimates, and proves (Theorem) that the estimator converges at rate O_p(n^{-r}) independent of dimension d, i.e., inherits the rate of a two-dimensional estimator. It validates the required assumptions for a kernel implementation (using a transformation-based bivariate copula kernel estimator), establishes asymptotic normality, and illustrates gains in simulations and an astrophysics classification problem.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not directly target the Gaussian Parzen window likelihood estimator itself: it does not analyze or reduce the variance of Parzen window estimates, and it does not examine the reliability of estimated "test likelihood" values (e.g., for scoring test points) in high dimensions. Instead it replaces kernel density estimation with a different structural model, and this only escapes the curse of dimensionality under the simplified vine copula assumption: when the true density is not a simplified vine distribution, the estimator is not consistent and converges to an approximation (the partial vine copula approximation), with performance advantages demonstrated only empirically in that misspecified case. Practical issues remain open for the gap: the vine structure is assumed known (only heuristic selection is discussed), the method estimates the full density rather than the Parzen-window test-likelihood quantity whose variance motivated the gap, and boundary/bounded-support and normalization aspects of likelihood evaluation are not directly treated.
evidence_snippets: We show that one can evade the curse of dimensionality by assuming a simplified vine copula model for the dependence between variables.

By \hyperref[Theory:rate_thm]{Theorem \ref*{Theory:rate_thm}}, the proposed vine copula based kernel density estimator inherits the convergence rate of the bivariate copula density estimator. It does not depend on the dimension $d$ and, therefore, suffers no curse of dimensionality.

We emphasize that a necessary condition for [REF:Theory:rate_thm] to hold with $r = p/(2p + 2)$ is that the density $f$ belongs to the class of simplified vine densities. If this is not the case, the estimator described in [REF:RVineKDE] is not consistent, but converges towards a simplified vine density that is merely an approximation of the true density.

paper.title: Breaking the curse of dimensionality in structured density estimation
paper.abstract: We consider the problem of estimating a structured multivariate density, subject to Markov conditions implied by an undirected graph. In the worst case, without Markovian assumptions, this problem suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Our main result shows how the curse of dimensionality can be avoided or greatly alleviated under the Markov property, and applies to arbitrary graphs. While existing results along these lines focus on sparsity or manifold assumptions, we introduce a new graphical quantity called "graph resilience" and show how it controls the sample complexity. Surprisingly, although one might expect the sample complexity of this problem to scale with local graph parameters such as the degree, this turns out not to be the case. Through explicit examples, we compute uniform deviation bounds and illustrate how the curse of dimensionality in density estimation can thus be circumvented. Notable examples where the rate improves substantially include sequential, hierarchical, and spatial data.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper is a theoretical study of the sample complexity of nonparametric density estimation for distributions that satisfy the Markov property with respect to an undirected graph. It introduces "graph resilience" r(G) as a measure of effective dimension and proves that the curse of dimensionality can be replaced by r(G) (rates ~(1/eps)^{r+2}) for arbitrary graphs, including when the graph is unknown. This bears on high-dimensional density estimation in general but concerns a histogram/covering-based estimator analyzed in TV distance, not any Parzen-window (kernel) likelihood estimator.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap — that the Gaussian Parzen window likelihood estimate has high variance and performs poorly in high dimensions — is not addressed at all. The paper neither studies Parzen/kernel density estimators nor estimates "test likelihood"; it proves minimax-style sample complexity results for Markov-structured densities using a histogram/discretization estimator and total-variation error. It does not propose, analyze, or improve the Parzen window method, and it does not address the variance or likelihood-reliability issues that define the gap. (If the gap were instead read broadly as "high-dimensional density estimation suffers the curse of dimensionality," the paper's Markov-graph assumption is an extra structural condition that the gap's setting does not presuppose, and it still says nothing about Parzen windows specifically.)

paper.title: High-dimensional density estimation with tensorizing flow
paper.abstract: We propose the tensorizing flow method for estimating high-dimensional probability density functions from the observed data. The method is based on tensor-train and flow-based generative modeling. Our method first efficiently constructs an approximate density in the tensor-train form via solving the tensor cores from a linear system based on the kernel density estimators of low-dimensional marginals. We then train a continuous-time flow model from this tensor-train density to the observed empirical distribution by performing a maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed method combines the optimization-less feature of the tensor-train with the flexibility of the flow-based generative models. Numerical results are included to demonstrate the performance of the proposed method.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes "tensorizing flow," a high-dimensional density estimation method that first constructs an approximate tensor-train (TT) density from samples (using sketching plus kernel density estimation only on 2- and 3-dimensional marginals) and then refines it with a continuous-time (ODE-based) flow model trained by maximum likelihood. Experiments on synthetic Rosenbrock and 1D/2D Ginzburg–Landau distributions (d = 8–16) show lower training/test loss and better generalization than normalizing flow. This is a generative density-estimation contribution in the broad area of high-dimensional likelihood estimation, but it does not target Parzen-window likelihood estimation for test data.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap — that the Gaussian Parzen-window (kernel density) likelihood estimate used to evaluate test likelihood has high variance and fails in high dimensions — is not addressed. The paper never uses or analyzes Parzen-window/KDE estimators as a means of estimating test likelihood in high dimensions, never quantifies their variance or failure mode, and does not compare its method against Parzen-window-based test-likelihood estimates. KDE appears only as an internal smoothing device for 2- and 3-marginals used to build the TT base distribution; the paper explicitly avoids full-dimensional KDE because of the curse of dimensionality, but proposes no analysis or replacement for the Parzen test-likelihood evaluation task itself. Moreover, its validation is limited to low/moderate-dimensional synthetic distributions (d = 8–16) on compact support I^d under (near-)Markovian assumptions, so the reliability of high-dimensional likelihood estimates in the gap's setting remains open.

paper.title: High-Dimensional Non-Parametric Density Estimation in Mixed Smooth Sobolev Spaces
paper.abstract: Density estimation plays a key role in many tasks in machine learning, statistical inference, and visualization. The main bottleneck in high-dimensional density estimation is the prohibitive computational cost and the slow convergence rate. In this paper, we propose novel estimators for high-dimensional non-parametric density estimation called the adaptive hyperbolic cross density estimators, which enjoys nice convergence properties in the mixed smooth Sobolev spaces. As modifications of the usual Sobolev spaces, the mixed smooth Sobolev spaces are more suitable for describing high-dimensional density functions in some applications. We prove that, unlike other existing approaches, the proposed estimator does not suffer the curse of dimensionality under Integral Probability Metric, including Hölder Integral Probability Metric, where Total Variation Metric and Wasserstein Distance are special cases. Applications of the proposed estimators to generative adversarial networks (GANs) and goodness of fit test for high-dimensional data are discussed to illustrate the proposed estimator's good performance in high-dimensional problems. Numerical experiments are conducted and illustrate the efficiency of our proposed method.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper argues that kernel density estimators (the family to which Gaussian Parzen windows belong) work poorly in high dimensions, and proposes a wavelet/orthogonal-series estimator called the adaptive hyperbolic cross estimator (AHCE). It proves that AHCE attains a nearly dimension-free (log-dependent) convergence rate under Integral Probability Metrics when the true density belongs to a mixed smooth Sobolev space, and applies it to GAN training and goodness-of-fit testing, with numerical results in D = 5–20 and MNIST. This is a genuine attempt to replace the unreliable high-dimensional kernel/Parzen-style density estimate with a better-behaved estimator.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the specific Gaussian Parzen window method used to estimate test likelihood, which has high variance and fails in high dimensions. This paper does not analyze Parzen-window likelihood estimation, pointwise likelihood evaluation, or the variance of test-likelihood estimates at all; it proposes a fundamentally different estimator whose near-dimension-free guarantees hold only under the strong structural assumption that the density lies in a mixed smooth Sobolev space (essentially tensor-product / near-product structure — indeed the numerical experiments use i.i.d. product-type Beta and t distributions). For general anisotropic or unstructured high-dimensional densities, the curse of dimensionality is not broken, and no reliable test-likelihood estimator is provided for the setting where Parzen windows are actually used. It also does not fix or improve the Gaussian Parzen window estimator itself.
evidence_snippets: However, the tuning bandwidth procedure and the slow converge rate make the kernel density estimator works poorly in high dimensional setting.

We propose a novel estimator adaptive hyperbolic cross estimator (AHCE) applied to high dimensional problems, which covers a large class of estimators. Under the mixed smooth Sobolev spaces, we show that the convergence rate of the proposed method under IPM loss is (nearly) dimension-free.

In contrast, our proposed approach suffers much less for it requires much less bases to achieve the same level of bias compared to other methods. The dimension $D$ only appears in the $\log$ term, and if $\beta$ satisfies some mild conditions, the convergence rate of our method is $n^{-1/2}$, which is { dimension-free} and is the optimal rate in learning problems.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Making real progress is feasible only in a scoped-down form: one can empirically characterize Parzen-window variance, propose variance-reduced or better bandwidth-selected Gaussian Parzen estimators, and benchmark them on synthetic densities in moderate dimensions using cheap compute and easily generated data, with clear metrics (MISE, KL, held-out log-likelihood variance). However, the gap as stated — "reliable in high dimensions" — runs into the fundamental curse of dimensionality for unstructured nonparametric density estimation; any genuine fix requires structural assumptions (sparsity, low-dimensional manifolds, vine/product structure), which changes the estimator rather than fixing plain Parzen windows. The validator's finding confirms prior work only partially circumvents this via structurally constrained alternatives. So it is not a fundamental-breakthrough-free, well-defined extension, but a focused empirical/methodological study is tractable.

verdicts.title: No claim of superiority over existing generative models
verdicts.description: The authors qualify their sample-quality results by stating that they make no claim the generated samples are better than those produced by existing methods, only that they are at least competitive with the better generative models in the literature.
verdicts.canonical_description: generated sample quality only claimed competitive, not superior to existing methods

evidence.anchor: we make no claim that these samples are better than
evidence.quote: While we make no claim that these samples are better than

verdict.reasoning: The gap is specifically the absence of a superiority claim for generated-sample quality (only "competitive" was claimed). Three deep-read papers squarely resolve this. Cooperative Training (CoT) explicitly reports state-of-the-art sample quality and diversity on discrete sequence generation (BLEU/n-gram metrics), asserting "superior performance" over all baselines at matched architecture capacity. Inclusive-NRFs claim to "consistently improve over state-of-the-art results" and back it with quantitative CIFAR-10 IS/FID scores. Splitting GAN likewise claims state-of-the-art Inception scores on CIFAR-10 and STL-10 in both supervised and unsupervised settings, describing images as "clearly better." These are direct, quantitative superiority claims over existing generative models, so the specific shortcoming identified in the gap is addressed. The two partial assessments (ARF's hedged "comparable or superior" on tabular data only, and Ways of Conditioning's superiority only over concatenation baselines via a density metric) do not undermine this: they are narrower in scope and remain hedged, but the central gap is covered by the stronger papers. Confidence is high because the direct-solution papers present concrete metrics rather than vague assertions; the only residual caveat is that a few superiority claims are tied to particular architectures/datasets rather than being unconditional across all scenarios.

paper.title: CoT: Cooperative Training for Generative Modeling of Discrete Data
paper.abstract: In this paper, we study the generative models of sequential discrete data. To tackle the exposure bias problem inherent in maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), generative adversarial networks (GANs) are introduced to penalize the unrealistic generated samples. To exploit the supervision signal from the discriminator, most previous models leverage REINFORCE to address the non-differentiable problem of sequential discrete data. However, because of the unstable property of the training signal during the dynamic process of adversarial training, the effectiveness of REINFORCE, in this case, is hardly guaranteed. To deal with such a problem, we propose a novel approach called Cooperative Training (CoT) to improve the training of sequence generative models. CoT transforms the min-max game of GANs into a joint maximization framework and manages to explicitly estimate and optimize Jensen-Shannon divergence. Moreover, CoT works without the necessity of pre-training via MLE, which is crucial to the success of previous methods. In the experiments, compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, CoT shows superior or at least competitive performance on sample quality, diversity, as well as training stability.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Cooperative Training (CoT) for sequence generation of discrete data and — in contrast to a paper that only claims competitiveness — explicitly asserts superiority over existing generative models. In synthetic experiments it states that its algorithm "reaches the state-of-the-art performance with exactly the same network architecture," and in real-data text generation it claims CoT-basic "achieves state-of-the-art performance over all the baselines" on quality (BLEU) and diversity metrics. The conclusion likewise states "CoT achieves superior performance on sample quality, diversity, as well as training stability," directly countering the gap's "no claim of superiority" weakness.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap (absence of a superiority claim for generated-sample quality) is directly addressed: the paper does claim state-of-the-art/superior sample quality and diversity over existing baselines in both synthetic and real-data experiments. The only residual hedging is that the abstract still phrases results as "superior or at least competitive," and the strongest superiority claims are tied to particular settings/architectures (e.g., same architecture-level capacity baselines, CoT-strong with an inverse-temperature strategy), so a fully unconditional, across-all-scenarios superiority claim is not made. But the central shortcoming identified by the gap — making no claim of superiority — is resolved.
evidence_snippets: In the experiments, compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, CoT shows superior or at least competitive performance on sample quality, diversity, as well as training stability.
We show that under this more reasonable setting, our proposed algorithm reaches the state-of-the-art performance with exactly the same network architecture.
In terms of generative quality, CoT-basic achieves state-of-the-art performance over all the baselines with the same architecture-level capacity, especially the long-term robustness at n-gram level.

paper.title: Generative Modeling by Inclusive Neural Random Fields with Applications in Image Generation and Anomaly Detection
paper.abstract: Neural random fields (NRFs), referring to a class of generative models that use neural networks to implement potential functions in random fields (a.k.a. energy-based models), are not new but receive less attention with slow progress. Different from various directed graphical models such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), NRFs provide an interesting family of undirected graphical models for generative modeling. In this paper we propose a new approach, the inclusive-NRF approach, to learning NRFs for continuous data (e.g. images), by introducing inclusive-divergence minimized auxiliary generators and developing stochastic gradient sampling in an augmented space. Based on the new approach, specific inclusive-NRF models are developed and thoroughly evaluated in two important generative modeling applications - image generation and anomaly detection. The proposed models consistently improve over state-of-the-art results in both applications. Remarkably, in addition to superior sample generation, one additional benefit of our inclusive-NRF approach is that, unlike GANs, it can directly provide (unnormalized) density estimate for sample evaluation. With these contributions and results, this paper significantly advances the learning and applications of NRFs to a new level, both theoretically and empirically, which have never been obtained before.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes inclusive-NRFs and, unlike a paper that only claims "competitive" sample quality, it explicitly claims and empirically demonstrates superiority over existing generative models. In image generation on CIFAR-10 it reports state-of-the-art Inception Score (IS 8.28, FID 20.9 with ResNet; IS 7.54, FID 27.9 with CNN) computed in the same way as the spectral-normalized GAN baselines, with the authors stating the models "consistently improve over state-of-the-art results." It also claims superior results in anomaly detection via density estimates.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper directly resolves the gap's core issue: rather than hedging generated-sample quality as merely competitive, it makes explicit superiority/state-of-the-art claims backed by IS/FID numbers. The only residual caveats are scope limitations that do not undermine the gap resolution: the sample-quality superiority claims are demonstrated on CIFAR-10 (and only against compared state-of-the-art methods with comparable architectures, mainly GAN/energy-model baselines), and on other datasets superiority is shown for anomaly detection rather than raw sample quality. Still, the specific problem of the gap — a missing superiority claim for generated sample quality — is addressed.
evidence_snippets: The proposed models consistently improve over state-of-the-art results in both applications.

Inclusive-NRFs achieve state-of-the-art sample generation quality, measured by both Inception Score (IS) and Frechet Inception Distance (FID), obtaining IS 8.28 (FID 20.9) with Resnet architecture [CITE:resnet] and {IS 7.54 (FID 27.9)} with CNN architecture [CITE:cnn] on CIFAR-10.
It is found that the inclusive-NRFs consistently improve over state-of-the-art results in both applications, which are summarized as follows.

paper.title: Class-Splitting Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) produce systematically better quality samples when class label information is provided., i.e. in the conditional GAN setup. This is still observed for the recently proposed Wasserstein GAN formulation which stabilized adversarial training and allows considering high capacity network architectures such as ResNet. In this work we show how to boost conditional GAN by augmenting available class labels. The new classes come from clustering in the representation space learned by the same GAN model. The proposed strategy is also feasible when no class information is available, i.e. in the unsupervised setup. Our generated samples reach state-of-the-art Inception scores for CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets in both supervised and unsupervised setup.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Splitting GAN, which augments class labels in a conditional WGAN-GP by k-means clustering in the critic's representation space, and it evaluates sample quality on CIFAR-10 and STL-10. Crucially for this gap, the paper does not stop at "competitive" claims: it explicitly claims superiority over existing generative models, reporting state-of-the-art Inception scores and stating that its images are "clearly better."
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific concern — that sample quality is only claimed competitive and not superior to existing methods — is directly addressed: the paper claims superior sample quality backed by Inception scores "well above the previous state-of-the-art" on both datasets, in both supervised and unsupervised settings. A minor residual caveat is that for unsupervised CIFAR-10 the paper acknowledges the Inception score is "similar" to the state-of-the-art and partly supports better quality by qualitative visual inspection ("samples generated seem to be of a higher quality"); however, its overall claim of superiority over existing generative models is explicit and quantitative.
evidence_snippets: Our generated samples reach state-of-the-art Inception scores for CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets in both supervised and unsupervised setup.

In this work we showed that our Splitting GAN method allows generating better images. This can be seen in the results on CIFAR-10 and STL-10 for which clearly better images were obtained. This is supported by an Inception score well above the previous state-of-the-art for both datasets.

paper.title: Adversarial random forests for density estimation and generative modeling
paper.abstract: We propose methods for density estimation and data synthesis using a novel form of unsupervised random forests. Inspired by generative adversarial networks, we implement a recursive procedure in which trees gradually learn structural properties of the data through alternating rounds of generation and discrimination. The method is provably consistent under minimal assumptions. Unlike classic tree-based alternatives, our approach provides smooth (un)conditional densities and allows for fully synthetic data generation. We achieve comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art probabilistic circuits and deep learning models on various tabular data benchmarks while executing about two orders of magnitude faster on average. An accompanying $\texttt{R}$ package, $\texttt{arf}$, is available on $\texttt{CRAN}$.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper introduces adversarial random forests (ARF) with Forde/Forge for density estimation and synthetic tabular data generation, and — unlike the gap's premise that only "competitive" quality is claimed — it explicitly asserts results that are at least competitive and in places superior to existing generative models. It claims "comparable or superior performance" to state-of-the-art probabilistic circuits and deep learning models on tabular benchmarks, reports Forge attaining the top accuracy/F1 in three of five tabular tasks against ctgan/tvae and tabular GAN variants, Forde dominating CART/PC-based baselines in NLL simulations, and orders-of-magnitude faster runtimes.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not fully solve the gap because it stops short of an unqualified claim that its generated samples are better than those of existing generative models. Its superiority assertions are hedged ("comparable or superior") and confined to specific settings: tabular classification benchmarks (accuracy/F1 as a proxy for sample fidelity), a simulation NLL study, and speed — while on the Twenty Datasets PC benchmark Forde only ranks second overall (best on two datasets), and no superiority over deep generative models for non-tabular/structured data is claimed. Thus the specific deficiency identified in the gap — establishing that generated sample quality is superior (not merely competitive) to existing generative models generally — is only partially and contextually addressed.
evidence_snippets: We achieve comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art probabilistic circuits and deep learning models on various tabular data benchmarks while executing about two orders of magnitude faster on average.
$Forge$ fares well in this experiment, attaining the top accuracy and F1-score in three out of five tasks.
Perhaps most impressive, $Forge$ executes over 60 times faster than its nearest competitor on average, and over 100 times faster than the second fastest method.

paper.title: Ways of Conditioning Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: The GANs are generative models whose random samples realistically reflect natural images. It also can generate samples with specific attributes by concatenating a condition vector into the input, yet research on this field is not well studied. We propose novel methods of conditioning generative adversarial networks (GANs) that achieve state-of-the-art results on MNIST and CIFAR-10. We mainly introduce two models: an information retrieving model that extracts conditional information from the samples, and a spatial bilinear pooling model that forms bilinear features derived from the spatial cross product of an image and a condition vector. These methods significantly enhance log-likelihood of test data under the conditional distributions compared to the methods of concatenation.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes two conditional-GAN conditioning mechanisms (Spatial Bilinear Pooling and Information Retrieving GAN) and evaluates them on MNIST and CIFAR-10 using Parzen-window log-likelihood of test data. It explicitly claims state-of-the-art results and superiority over the concatenation-based conditioning baselines it compares against (CGAN and FCGAN), reporting that SBP "surpass[es] CGAN and FCGAN" and that methods "significantly enhance log-likelihood ... compared to the methods of concatenation."
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper's superiority claims are limited in scope relative to the gap. First, its demonstrated superiority is only over two concatenation-based conditioning baselines (CGAN, FCGAN) sharing the same generator structure, not over the broader set of existing generative models in the literature, and the "state-of-the-art" claim is not backed by comparisons to those models. Second, the evidence is a quantitative density metric (Parzen-window log-likelihood of test data), not a claim or demonstration that generated sample quality (visual fidelity) is superior; there is no human evaluation or direct sample-quality comparison. Third, the authors concede the result is not uniform ("IRGAN ... didn't perform well on CIFAR-10 due to inaccurate classifier Q(c|x)") and call for further experiments. Thus the paper partially addresses the gap (it does make superiority claims over the compared conditioning methods) but does not establish that its generated samples are superior to existing generative models in general.
evidence_snippets: We propose novel methods of conditioning generative adversarial networks (GANs) that achieve state-of-the-art results on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
These methods significantly enhance log-likelihood of test data under the conditional distributions compared to the methods of concatenation.
We found that SBP showed stable results on both datasets and most of the labels, surpassing CGAN and FCGAN.

verdicts.title: Need for evaluation methods for likelihood-free generative models
verdicts.description: Generative models that can sample but cannot estimate likelihood directly motivate further research into how to evaluate such models.
verdicts.canonical_description: evaluation methods needed for generative models that sample without likelihood estimation

evidence.anchor: further research into how to evaluate such models
evidence.quote:
Advances in generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood directly motivate further research
into how to evaluate such models.

verdict.reasoning: The gap asks for evaluation methods for generative models that sample without likelihood estimation, and the subsequent literature supplies multiple direct solutions. PQMass provides a general, likelihood-free statistical framework that compares model and reference samples via Voronoi-region multinomial counts and Pearson chi-squared tests, requiring only distances, and is validated across images, tabular data, time series, and protein sequences with asymptotic consistency guarantees. The optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy paper contributes a two-sample test with power-optimized kernels, permutation null estimation, and witness visualization, validated on a real likelihood-free GAN. The latent-density-score paper adds a per-sample quality signal for latent-based generators (VAE, GAN, latent diffusion) without any pretrained feature extractor. Together these establish concrete, empirically validated methods for exactly the setting in the gap. Remaining caveats — i.i.d. sample requirements, reliance on a meaningful distance/kernel, needing a reference dataset or an encodable latent space, and limited coverage of modalities like language or correlated samplers — are limitations of individual methods rather than an unaddressed core problem; the canonical need for likelihood-free evaluation is substantially met. Confidence is high but not maximal because no single method is universal and a few modality-specific settings remain thinner.

paper.title: PQMass: Probabilistic Assessment of the Quality of Generative Models using Probability Mass Estimation
paper.abstract: We propose a likelihood-free method for comparing two distributions given samples from each, with the goal of assessing the quality of generative models. The proposed approach, PQMass, provides a statistically rigorous method for assessing the performance of a single generative model or the comparison of multiple competing models. PQMass divides the sample space into non-overlapping regions and applies chi-squared tests to the number of data samples that fall within each region, giving a p-value that measures the probability that the bin counts derived from two sets of samples are drawn from the same multinomial distribution. PQMass does not depend on assumptions regarding the density of the true distribution, nor does it rely on training or fitting any auxiliary models. We evaluate PQMass on data of various modalities and dimensions, demonstrating its effectiveness in assessing the quality, novelty, and diversity of generated samples. We further show that PQMass scales well to moderately high-dimensional data and thus obviates the need for feature extraction in practical applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes PQMass, a likelihood-free statistical framework for evaluating generative models by comparing two sets of samples (model-generated vs. reference). It partitions the space into Voronoi regions, counts how many samples fall in each region (a multinomial summary), and uses Pearson chi-squared tests to obtain a p-value assessing whether the two sample sets come from the same distribution. The method requires only distances between points — no likelihood, no density assumptions, and no auxiliary model fitting — which is exactly the setting described by the gap (generative models that sample but cannot estimate likelihood). The paper validates it empirically across modalities (sampling benchmarks, MNIST/CIFAR/FFHQ/ImageNet images, astrophysics images, time series, tabular data, protein sequences) and gives consistency guarantees that the test distinguishes distinct distributions asymptotically.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific problem — providing an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models — is substantially solved by this single well-tested proposal. Still, the paper itself documents residual gaps in coverage: the formalism requires i.i.d. samples (so models producing correlated samples cannot be evaluated); results are too noisy when sample counts are limited; effectiveness depends on a meaningful distance metric (nontrivial for modalities such as natural language); and novelty/memorization is only measured indirectly (via a two-sided/overfit p-value and generalization gap) rather than as a direct scalar. These are limitations of one method rather than an unaddressed part of the core problem.
evidence_snippets: We propose a likelihood-free method for comparing two distributions given samples from each, with the goal of assessing the quality of generative models.
PQMass does not depend on assumptions regarding the density of the true distribution, nor does it rely on training or fitting any auxiliary models.

In this work, we propose \name, a statistical framework for evaluating the quality of generative models that measures the combination of fidelity, diversity, and novelty and scales well to moderately high dimensions, without the need of dimensionality reduction.

paper.title: Generative Models and Model Criticism via Optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy
paper.abstract: We propose a method to optimize the representation and distinguishability of samples from two probability distributions, by maximizing the estimated power of a statistical test based on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). This optimized MMD is applied to the setting of unsupervised learning by generative adversarial networks (GAN), in which a model attempts to generate realistic samples, and a discriminator attempts to tell these apart from data samples. In this context, the MMD may be used in two roles: first, as a discriminator, either directly on the samples, or on features of the samples. Second, the MMD can be used to evaluate the performance of a generative model, by testing the model's samples against a reference data set. In the latter role, the optimized MMD is particularly helpful, as it gives an interpretable indication of how the model and data distributions differ, even in cases where individual model samples are not easily distinguished either by eye or by classifier.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper develops an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models (specifically GANs that sample but cannot compute likelihoods): an optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy two-sample test whose kernel/features are chosen by maximizing test power, together with efficient permutation null-distribution computation and witness-function visualization for model criticism. It demonstrates this evaluation approach on a real semi-supervised GAN trained on MNIST (discretized to {0,1}^{28x28}), showing it detects distributional discrepancies (e.g., overproduction of certain digit types and pixel-level artifacts) that human observers and the median-heuristic RBF MMD would miss, and also proposes MMD-based GAN training criteria.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper's solution is an evaluation methodology based on two-sample hypothesis testing of a trained model's samples against a reference data set. It does not address evaluation in settings where no reference data set or clean data/model distinction exists, nor does it provide a full comparative benchmark across many models or cover other evaluation facets (e.g., coverage/recall-style metrics, diversity-mode collapse quantification beyond what MMD captures, or evaluation without any available true samples). Within reference-data sample-based evaluation for likelihood-free generative models, the paper does substantially solve the stated problem and validates it empirically.
evidence_snippets: In light of these varied approaches to discriminator training, it is important to be able to evaluate quality of samples from a generator against reference data.
Second, the \acro{mmd} can be used to evaluate the performance of a generative model, by testing the model's samples against a reference data set.
As an example of a real-world two-sample testing problem, we will consider distinguishing the output of a generative model from the reference distribution it attempts to reproduce.

paper.title: Assessing Sample Quality via the Latent Space of Generative Models
paper.abstract: Advances in generative models increase the need for sample quality assessment. To do so, previous methods rely on a pre-trained feature extractor to embed the generated samples and real samples into a common space for comparison. However, different feature extractors might lead to inconsistent assessment outcomes. Moreover, these methods are not applicable for domains where a robust, universal feature extractor does not yet exist, such as medical images or 3D assets. In this paper, we propose to directly examine the latent space of the trained generative model to infer generated sample quality. This is feasible because the quality a generated sample directly relates to the amount of training data resembling it, and we can infer this information by examining the density of the latent space. Accordingly, we use a latent density score function to quantify sample quality. We show that the proposed score correlates highly with the sample quality for various generative models including VAEs, GANs and Latent Diffusion Models. Compared with previous quality assessment methods, our method has the following advantages: 1) pre-generation quality estimation with reduced computational cost, 2) generalizability to various domains and modalities, and 3) applicability to latent-based image editing and generation methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed methods can benefit downstream tasks such as few-shot image classification and latent face image editing. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/LS-sample-quality.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes an evaluation method for exactly the class of models in the gap: generative models (VAEs, GANs, Latent Diffusion Models, Stable Diffusion) that generate samples without providing likelihood estimates. Rather than requiring likelihood or a pretrained feature extractor, it scores each generated sample by the density of training-set latent codes around the sample's latent code in the generative model's own latent space ("latent density score"). The authors validate that this score correlates with per-sample visual quality, precision/recall, realism score, and truncation level, and show it generalizes to domains without universal feature extractors (medical/anime images, 3D shapes) and enables downstream tasks (few-shot classification, latent face editing). This directly provides an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fills the gap for instance-wise/per-sample quality assessment of latent-based likelihood-free generators, but it does not cover all ways one might "evaluate" such models. It does not provide a model-wise, distribution-level comparison metric (e.g., a FID-like aggregate of the whole generative distribution versus the real distribution); its score is a per-sample ranking/quality signal. Moreover, the method requires access to a generative model with a well-defined latent space into which real training samples can be encoded (or otherwise mapped to latent codes) plus a set of training latent codes, so it is not applicable to samplers lacking an encodable/invertible latent space or where training latent codes are unavailable. The authors explicitly leave high-dimensional latent models (e.g., deep hierarchical VAEs) and video/temporal latent generative models to future work, noting latent dimension reduction "might be a potential solution." For the core stated problem—evaluating models that sample without likelihood—the paper offers a concrete, validated solution.
evidence_snippets: we propose to directly examine the latent space of the trained generative model to infer generated sample quality.
We show that the proposed score correlates highly with the sample quality for various generative models including VAEs, GANs and Latent Diffusion Models.
In this paper, we propose to assess sample quality from another perspective: instead of using a pre-trained feature space, we directly use the latent space of the generative models themselves.

paper.title: Evaluating Generative Models for Tabular Data: Novel Metrics and Benchmarking
paper.abstract: Generative models have revolutionized multiple domains, yet their application to tabular data remains underexplored. Evaluating generative models for tabular data presents unique challenges due to structural complexity, large-scale variability, and mixed data types, making it difficult to intuitively capture intricate patterns. Existing evaluation metrics offer only partial insights, lacking a comprehensive measure of generative performance. To address this limitation, we propose three novel evaluation metrics: FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS. Our extensive experimental analysis, conducted on three standard network intrusion detection datasets, compares these metrics with established evaluation methods such as Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS. Our results demonstrate that FAED effectively captures generative modeling issues overlooked by existing metrics. While FPCAD exhibits promising performance, further refinements are necessary to enhance its reliability. Our proposed framework provides a robust and practical approach for assessing generative models in tabular data applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly tackles the likelihood-free evaluation problem by proposing sample-based evaluation metrics (FAED, FPCAD, RFIS) for generative models whose learned distribution is not explicitly accessible, i.e., models that can sample but not compute likelihoods. It adapts FID-like and IS-like principles to tabular data and benchmarks the new metrics against SDV Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS on three intrusion-detection datasets under injected quality decrease, mode drop, and mode collapse, finding FAED the most robust. This is a concrete instance of the requested evaluation methodology, but scoped to tabular generative models.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is general ("likelihood-free generative models" across domains), whereas this paper provides evaluation metrics only for tabular data, and only validates them on network intrusion detection datasets; the authors themselves call for extending FAED/RFIS beyond this domain. Moreover, the validation protocol does not evaluate outputs of actual trained likelihood-free generative models — instead it injects noise/mode drop/mode collapse into real test data and checks metric sensitivity — so evidence on real generative-model outputs remains open. Finally, the proposed metrics are not fully reliable solutions: FPCAD is inconsistent across datasets and RFIS is unreliable for mode drop, so a robust, generally applicable likelihood-free evaluation method is still not established.
evidence_snippets: Since the model's learned distribution is not explicitly accessible, direct validation becomes impractical.
Inspired by IS and FID, we introduce three novel evaluation metrics, FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS, tailored for assessing generative models in tabular data.
Among the proposed novel metrics, FAED emerged as the most robust, consistently detecting structural distortions in generated data across various degradation scenarios.

paper.title: Evaluation Metrics and Methods for Generative Models in the Wireless PHY Layer
paper.abstract: Generative models are typically evaluated by direct inspection of their generated samples, e.g., by visual inspection in the case of images. Further evaluation metrics like the Fréchet inception distance or maximum mean discrepancy are intricate to interpret and lack physical motivation. These observations make evaluating generative models in the wireless PHY layer non-trivial. This work establishes a framework consisting of evaluation metrics and methods for generative models applied to the wireless PHY layer. The proposed metrics and methods are motivated by wireless applications, facilitating interpretation and understandability for the wireless community. In particular, we propose a spectral efficiency analysis for validating the generated channel norms and a codebook fingerprinting method to validate the generated channel directions. Moreover, we propose an application cross-check to evaluate the generative model's samples for training machine learning-based models in relevant downstream tasks. Our analysis is based on real-world measurement data and includes the Gaussian mixture model, variational autoencoder, diffusion model, and generative adversarial network as generative models. Our results under a fair comparison in terms of model architecture indicate that solely relying on metrics like the maximum mean discrepancy produces insufficient evaluation outcomes. In contrast, the proposed metrics and methods exhibit consistent and explainable behavior.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes three sample-only evaluation routines for generative models trained on wireless PHY channel data: (1) a spectral-efficiency analysis (empirical SE CDFs + Wasserstein distance) that validates generated channel norms, (2) a codebook-fingerprinting method (histograms over DFT-codebook indices compared via total variation distance) that validates generated channel directions, and (3) an application cross-check in which downstream models (GMM/VAE channel estimators and an autoencoder for channel compression) are trained on generated versus real (RPE) data and compared on the same test set. Because every routine uses only generated samples and never requires likelihood values, the framework is applicable to likelihood-free/implicit models and is demonstrated on GMM, VAE, diffusion model, and WGAN using real-world measurements.
assessments.what_remains_open: The research gap is generic: evaluation methods for likelihood-free generative models that sample without estimating likelihood. This paper provides a domain-specific instantiation only — all proposed metrics and methods are tied to wireless PHY channel data and its physical structure (channel-norm-driven SE, DFT-codebook direction histograms, communications downstream tasks such as channel estimation/compression). It does not provide a general, domain-agnostic evaluation methodology or transferable principle for assessing arbitrary likelihood-free generative models (e.g., image/text/tabular data), nor statistical guarantees or sample-complexity bounds for the proposed checks. Within wireless PHY it also evaluates one measurement scenario/config, and the authors note the rankings depend on the system configuration, so a generally applicable evaluation recipe for likelihood-free models remains open.
evidence_snippets: As a result, there is no clear guideline for assessing the quality of a generated channel with an established metric. Therefore, we propose a framework consisting of several evaluation metrics and methods for generative models in this work that are specifically suited for wireless channel data.

We propose an \ac{se} analysis and codebook fingerprinting as evaluation routines, allowing us to assess whether the generative model can capture two important channel properties for PHY layer algorithms: the overall channel power and directional information.

We introduce a general framework for an application cross-check. The cross-check enables us to determine if a generative model can be utilized in place of the true \ac{rpe} data for training \ac{ml}-based PHY layer methods and generate authentic channels.

verdicts.title: Optimizing discriminator to completion is prohibitive
verdicts.description: Optimizing D to completion in the inner loop of training is computationally prohibitive and would result in overfitting on finite datasets, so an iterative alternation must be used instead.
verdicts.canonical_description: full inner-loop discriminator optimization computationally prohibitive and overfits

evidence.anchor: in the inner loop of training is computationally prohibitive
evidence.quote:
Optimizing $D$ to completion in the
inner loop of training is computationally prohibitive,

verdict.reasoning: All three deep-read papers are assessed as not_addressed, and the assessments are consistent and specific. Paper 1 analyzes GAN generalization and equilibrium while taking the alternating training protocol as given; its best-response cycling examples concern non-convergence of full optimization, not the computational cost or finite-sample overfitting of completing the inner-loop discriminator update. Paper 2 is diagnostic work on discriminator under/overfitting in WGANs, but its independent discriminator is trained offline for measurement after the generator is fixed, not as a replacement for or mitigation of full inner-loop optimization. Paper 3 reframes GANs as a Lagrangian saddle-point problem and proves convergence of alternating primal-dual updates, but again assumes the standard single-step alternation and abstracts away finite-capacity/finite-data regimes. None of the papers analyzes why full inner-loop discriminator optimization is computationally prohibitive, characterizes an appropriate number of discriminator steps, proposes a feasible scheme for optimizing D to completion, or justifies the alternation schedule. The gap's specific problem therefore remains untouched.

paper.title: Generalization and Equilibrium in Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs)
paper.abstract: We show that training of generative adversarial network (GAN) may not have good generalization properties; e.g., training may appear successful but the trained distribution may be far from target distribution in standard metrics. However, generalization does occur for a weaker metric called neural net distance. It is also shown that an approximate pure equilibrium exists in the discriminator/generator game for a special class of generators with natural training objectives when generator capacity and training set sizes are moderate. This existence of equilibrium inspires MIX+GAN protocol, which can be combined with any existing GAN training, and empirically shown to improve some of them.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper is a GAN theory paper on two distinct questions: (1) whether GAN training generalizes, showing that JS/Wasserstein distances can fail to generalize on finite samples while a weaker "neural net distance" does generalize, and (2) whether approximate pure equilibria exist in the generator/discriminator game, proved for mixtures of generators and for enlarged (k+1-layer, ~p^2 parameter) generator nets, plus the heuristic MIX+GAN. It also gives toy examples where best-response dynamics (optimizing each player to optimality) cycle and fail to converge. None of these contributions addresses how or whether to optimize the discriminator to completion in the inner loop, or why an iterative alternation must be used instead.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap — that full inner-loop discriminator optimization is computationally prohibitive and would overfit on finite datasets, so iterative alternation must be used — is not tackled. The paper takes the standard alternating training procedure as given and analyzes its generalization and equilibrium properties; it does not analyze the computational cost of running D to completion, does not characterize how many (k) discriminator steps suffice, does not propose or justify an alternation schedule, and does not connect the finite-sample overfitting failure modes it identifies (JS/Wasserstein memorization, low-capacity discriminators missing diversity) to the burden of completing the inner-loop D optimization. Its best-response examples concern non-convergence/cycling of full optimization rather than computational prohibitive-ness or finite-sample overfitting of the inner-loop D update.

paper.title: Investigating Under and Overfitting in Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: We investigate under and overfitting in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), using discriminators unseen by the generator to measure generalization. We find that the model capacity of the discriminator has a significant effect on the generator's model quality, and that the generator's poor performance coincides with the discriminator underfitting. Contrary to our expectations, we find that generators with large model capacities relative to the discriminator do not show evidence of overfitting on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CelebA.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper is an empirical study of under/overfitting in Wasserstein GANs. It introduces auxiliary and independent discriminators (trained on data unseen by the generator, or on an independent held-out split) to measure discriminator generalization and generator model quality, and it varies discriminator capacity. Its main findings are that the alternation-trained original discriminator underfits/fails to generalize on test data while auxiliary/independent discriminators show little generalization gap, and that generator overfitting is not observed on CIFAR10/100/CelebA. This is adjacent diagnostic work about discriminator generalization, but it does not address the problem of making full inner-loop discriminator optimization tractable during GAN training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that optimizing the discriminator to completion in the inner loop of GAN training is computationally prohibitive and would overfit finite datasets, so iterative alternation is required — is not addressed. The paper never proposes or evaluates a procedure for full inner-loop discriminator optimization while training the generator; its "independent discriminator" is trained offline (100K SGD steps) after a generator is fixed, purely to estimate a divergence for measurement, not to replace the inner-loop optimization. It likewise does nothing to mitigate the computational cost of full discriminator training or to justify reducing the number of alternation steps. Thus the question of how to make full inner-loop discriminator optimization feasible, or how to avoid the overfitting/prohibitive-cost tradeoff that motivates alternation, remains entirely open.

paper.title: Training Generative Adversarial Networks via Primal-Dual Subgradient Methods: A Lagrangian Perspective on GAN
paper.abstract: We relate the minimax game of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to finding the saddle points of the Lagrangian function for a convex optimization problem, where the discriminator outputs and the distribution of generator outputs play the roles of primal variables and dual variables, respectively. This formulation shows the connection between the standard GAN training process and the primal-dual subgradient methods for convex optimization. The inherent connection does not only provide a theoretical convergence proof for training GANs in the function space, but also inspires a novel objective function for training. The modified objective function forces the distribution of generator outputs to be updated along the direction according to the primal-dual subgradient methods. A toy example shows that the proposed method is able to resolve mode collapse, which in this case cannot be avoided by the standard GAN or Wasserstein GAN. Experiments on both Gaussian mixture synthetic data and real-world image datasets demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on generating diverse samples.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper reinterprets the GAN minimax game as finding saddle points of the Lagrangian of a convex program (discriminator outputs as primal variables, generator-output distribution as dual variables), proves convergence of alternating primal-dual subgradient updates in function space when discriminator/generator have enough capacity, and proposes a modified generator loss that pushes the generated probability distribution along the optimal dual direction to mitigate mode collapse. Its main contributions are theoretical convergence guarantees (in an idealized convex, full-capacity setting) and a mode-collapse-avoiding training objective, validated on toy/Gaussian-mixture data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the reason full inner-loop discriminator optimization is infeasible — computational cost and overfitting on finite datasets — and the consequent need for iterative alternation. The paper does not analyze or address this problem: it takes the standard alternating protocol as given (k0 = 1 single-step discriminator updates in all experiments), never studies the cost or the overfitting induced by training D to completion, and does not propose any scheme or analysis related to discriminator overfitting on finite data. Its convergence theorem instead assumes an idealized function-space convex optimization with full-capacity networks and an adequate step-size schedule, assumptions that abstract away precisely the finite-capacity/finite-data regime where the gap's problem arises. Mode collapse (a different failure mode) is the actual target of the proposed generator-objective change, so the specific problem in this gap remains untouched.

verdicts.title: MLP generator lacks theoretical guarantees
verdicts.description: Using a multilayer perceptron to define G introduces multiple critical points in parameter space, so adversarial nets lack theoretical guarantees despite their good practical performance.
verdicts.canonical_description: multilayer perceptron parameterization introduces multiple critical points and lacks theoretical guarantees
