verdict.reasoning: The three papers jointly move some theory from the infinite-capacity setting toward finite-capacity networks, but none delivers global-optimality or training-convergence guarantees for finite-capacity MLPs. Paper 1 gives finite-sample statistical rates for neural-net generator/discriminator pairs, yet these are oracle bounds for the idealized empirical minimax estimator, with no optimization analysis and with fast rates tied to realizable architectures. Paper 2 is still largely nonparametric; its finite ReLU-network results only approximate infinite-capacity Sobolev classes and explicitly exclude the optimization side. Paper 3 is the most direct: it proves finite-parameter generalization for a weaker neural-net distance, shows standard metrics cannot generalize polynomially, and establishes an approximate pure equilibrium for a specially constructed augmented architecture. However, that is an existence result, not a convergence result for any training algorithm, and it still routes through infinite mixtures before folding them into a finite net. Thus the gap's specific demand — global optimality and convergence established directly for finite-capacity multilayer perceptrons — remains substantively open even though finite-capacity statistical and equilibrium-existence results now exist.

paper.title: How Well Generative Adversarial Networks Learn Distributions
paper.abstract: This paper studies the rates of convergence for learning distributions implicitly with the adversarial framework and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which subsume Wasserstein, Sobolev, MMD GAN, and Generalized/Simulated Method of Moments (GMM/SMM) as special cases. We study a wide range of parametric and nonparametric target distributions under a host of objective evaluation metrics. We investigate how to obtain valid statistical guarantees for GANs through the lens of regularization. On the nonparametric end, we derive the optimal minimax rates for distribution estimation under the adversarial framework. On the parametric end, we establish a theory for general neural network classes (including deep leaky ReLU networks) that characterizes the interplay on the choice of generator and discriminator pair. We discover and isolate a new notion of regularization, called the generator-discriminator-pair regularization, that sheds light on the advantage of GANs compared to classical parametric and nonparametric approaches for explicit distribution estimation. We develop novel oracle inequalities as the main technical tools for analyzing GANs, which are of independent interest.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper provides a statistical (finite-sample, rate-based) theory for GANs. Besides the nonparametric adversarial framework (Sobolev, RKHS/MMD, GMM/SMM minimax rates), it devotes an entire section to GANs whose generator and discriminator are finite-capacity neural networks, deriving oracle-inequality rates under TV/KL/Wasserstein metrics with explicit dependence on the pseudo-dimensions Pdim(F) and Pdim(F∘G), and showing near-optimal sample complexity for realizable deep leaky ReLU generators and multivariate Gaussians with two-layer networks. Thus it gives theoretical guarantees directly for finite-capacity multilayer perceptrons rather than only in the infinite-capacity nonparametric setting.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's "global optimality and convergence" is only partially addressed. The paper's guarantees are statistical convergence rates for the idealized empirical minimax estimator \hat\theta_{m,n} (argmin of the empirical max-min objective), not proofs that a finite-capacity MLP training algorithm actually converges to a global optimum of the nonconvex GAN game; no optimization/training-dynamics analysis is given. Moreover, the fast parametric rates for finite-capacity networks are oracle-type bounds whose approximation terms A1(F,G,ν) and A2(G,ν) only vanish when the log-density ratios are exactly realizable/approximable by the specific network architectures (deep leaky ReLU / quadratic-activation constructions), so global-optimality-type guarantees are not obtained for arbitrary finite-capacity MLPs. The minimax-optimal (lower-bound matching) results themselves remain in the infinite-capacity nonparametric setting.
evidence_snippets: In this section, we consider when both the generator and discriminator are parameterized by neural networks, and derive rates applicable to GAN used in practice (as well as SMM).

(1) we derive the parametric rates on the closeness between the implicit distribution estimator (distribution of $g_{\widehat{\theta}_{m,n}}(Z)$) and the target $\nu$ under objective metrics, when both $\G$ and $\F$ are parametrized by general neural networks;

(a) learning distributions realizable by deep leaky ReLU networks, and (b) learning multivariate Gaussian distributions with two-layer networks. In both cases, the upper rates we obtain provide optimal sample complexity (up to logarithmic factors).

paper.title: How Well Can Generative Adversarial Networks Learn Densities: A Nonparametric View
paper.abstract: We study in this paper the rate of convergence for learning densities under the Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) framework, borrowing insights from nonparametric statistics. We introduce an improved GAN estimator that achieves a faster rate, through simultaneously leveraging the level of smoothness in the target density and the evaluation metric, which in theory remedies the mode collapse problem reported in the literature. A minimax lower bound is constructed to show that when the dimension is large, the exponent in the rate for the new GAN estimator is near optimal. One can view our results as answering in a quantitative way how well GAN learns a wide range of densities with different smoothness properties, under a hierarchy of evaluation metrics. As a byproduct, we also obtain improved generalization bounds for GAN with deeper ReLU discriminator network.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper derives minimax convergence rates for GAN-based density estimation, mostly in a fully nonparametric (Sobolev-space) framework: upper bounds via smoothed empirical measures when target density is in W^{α,2} and the discriminator class is W^{β,2}, plus matching minimax lower bounds. It also contains one section that moves toward finite networks: a rate bound when the discriminator is a finite-depth ReLU network F^{(ℓ)}(V), and guarantees when discriminator/generator network classes approximate Sobolev classes within ε. However, these results are statistical rates for the oracle GAN estimator, and the finite-network treatment still relies on networks approximating infinite-capacity nonparametric classes.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns guarantees for finite-capacity MLPs — in particular global optimality and convergence — instead of relying on an infinite-capacity nonparametric setting. This paper does not close that gap: (1) its central theorems are themselves stated for nonparametric classes (target densities and discriminators in Sobolev spaces, generator handled only through the abstract approximation error min_{μ∈μ_G} d_{F_D}(μ,ν)), i.e., exactly the infinite-capacity setting; (2) it explicitly excludes the optimization side, so it gives no global-optimality or training-dynamics convergence results for fixed finite-capacity MLPs; (3) where ReLU networks appear, the bounds contain an approximation error term ε and attaining the stated nonparametric rate requires network size to grow with n (depth O(log n), units poly(n) / ε^{-d/β}), which is again the infinite-capacity limit rather than guarantees for a fixed finite-capacity architecture; (4) the generator is never treated as a finite MLP producing a transformed distribution, only as approximating densities in sup-norm. Thus part of the gap (finite ReLU discriminators with bounded weights get an improved statistical bound) is touched, but the specific problem — theoretical global optimality/convergence established directly for finite-capacity MLPs — remains open.
evidence_snippets: The focus of the current paper is not on the optimization side of how to solve for $\tilde{\mu}_n$ efficiently, rather on the statistical front: how well $\tilde{\mu}_n$ estimates a wide range of nonparametric distributions $\nu$ under a wide collection of objective metrics

Roughly, this means that one may need a deep discriminator network (scales logarithmically with number of samples in depth, and polynomially in number of units) to recover the density in a strong sense such as under the Wasserstein metric.

paper.title: Generalization and Equilibrium in Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs)
paper.abstract: We show that training of generative adversarial network (GAN) may not have good generalization properties; e.g., training may appear successful but the trained distribution may be far from target distribution in standard metrics. However, generalization does occur for a weaker metric called neural net distance. It is also shown that an approximate pure equilibrium exists in the discriminator/generator game for a special class of generators with natural training objectives when generator capacity and training set sizes are moderate. This existence of equilibrium inspires MIX+GAN protocol, which can be combined with any existing GAN training, and empirically shown to improve some of them.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly confronts the reliance on non-parametric/infinite-capacity analysis: it shows that standard-metric guarantees obtained by choosing the optimal discriminator over all functions (or all 1-Lipschitz functions) fail to generalize with polynomial samples, and instead proves generalization bounds for a "neural net distance" where the discriminator class is a finite-parameter (p-parameter) neural net. It also gives an existence theorem for an approximate pure equilibrium: starting from infinite mixtures, it shows O~(p/eps^2) generators suffice, and then folds the mixture into a single (k+1)-layer neural network with O(p^2) parameters, yielding an epsilon-approximate pure equilibrium for finite-capacity nets. Thus parts of the theory are moved from the infinite-capacity non-parametric regime to explicit finite-capacity statements.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap asks for global-optimality/convergence theory stated directly for finite-capacity multilayer perceptrons, and this paper does not fully deliver that. The finite-capacity guarantees it obtains are under clear limitations: (1) the generalization guarantee holds only for the weaker neural-net distance, while the paper proves that in standard metrics (JS, Wasserstein) a finite-capacity/parametric setup cannot generalize with polynomial samples, so the usual "generator wins => D close to D_real" optimality statement is not rescued; (2) the approximate pure equilibrium exists only for a specially constructed, augmented architecture — a k+1-layer net with multiway selectors and O(p^2) parameters — and the authors state it is open whether pure equilibria exist for the original structured (e.g., convolutional) architectures; (3) it is an existence theorem for an equilibrium, not a convergence result for any training algorithm, and the paper even shows best-response training can fail to converge (cycle) with finite capacity; (4) the equilibrium argument still passes first through infinite mixtures and then approximates them. So the specific problem of providing global optimality/convergence guarantees directly for standard finite-capacity MLP training remains open.
evidence_snippets: in the discriminator/generator game for a special class of generators with natural training objectives when generator capacity and training set sizes are moderate

there exists $k+1$-layer neural networks of generators $G$ and discriminator $D$ with $O\left(\frac{\Delta^2 p^2\log (L L' L_{\phi}\cdot p/\epsilon)}{\epsilon^2}\right)$ parameters, such that there exists an $\epsilon$-approximate pure equilibrium with value $2\phi(1/2)$
It is left for future work whether pure equilibria exist for the original structured architectures.

verdict.reasoning: The gap describes the proposal that conditioning a generative model can be achieved by feeding the conditioning variable into both the generator and discriminator. The deep-read paper — Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets — is precisely this contribution. It formally introduces conditioning by feeding y into both the generator and discriminator, states the resulting two-player minimax objective over D(x|y) and G(z|y), and validates the construction empirically on class-conditioned MNIST digits and MIR Flickr image-tag generation. The limitations noted in the assessment (proof-of-concept accuracy on MNIST, preliminary multi-modal results, single-tag conditioning, and joint language-model training left to future work) concern the maturity and breadth of results, not the gap's specific mechanism. Since the proposed extension is directly formalized and demonstrated, the gap is fully addressed. Confidence is high because the evidence squarely matches the gap's exact statement, though it rests on a single paper and the empirical results are acknowledged as preliminary.

paper.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Nets
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Nets [8] were recently introduced as a novel way to train generative models. In this work we introduce the conditional version of generative adversarial nets, which can be constructed by simply feeding the data, y, we wish to condition on to both the generator and discriminator. We show that this model can generate MNIST digits conditioned on class labels. We also illustrate how this model could be used to learn a multi-modal model, and provide preliminary examples of an application to image tagging in which we demonstrate how this approach can generate descriptive tags which are not part of training labels.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper is precisely the work that proposed the extension described in the gap: it introduces conditional generative adversarial nets by feeding the conditioning variable y into both the generator and the discriminator, and formalizes the resulting two-player minimax objective (D(x|y), G(z|y)). It implements and demonstrates the idea with experiments on MNIST digit generation conditioned on class labels and on MIR Flickr image-tag generation for multi-modal modeling.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — proposing and validating that conditioning c can be added as input to both generator and discriminator to obtain a conditional generative model — is fully addressed by this paper, which even demonstrates the construction empirically. What the paper itself leaves open is not the proposed mechanism but rather its efficacy and maturity: the authors state the MNIST results are a "proof-of-concept" that are outperformed by several other approaches including non-conditional adversarial nets, the multi-modal tag-generation results are preliminary, tags are used only individually rather than jointly, and joint training of the language model is left to future work. These are refinements beyond the gap's stated scope.
evidence_snippets: Generative adversarial nets can be extended to a conditional model if both the generator and discriminator are conditioned on some extra information ${\bm{y}}$.
We can perform the conditioning by feeding ${\bm{y}}$ into the both the discriminator and generator as additional input layer.

In this work we introduce the conditional version of generative adversarial nets, which can be constructed by simply feeding the data, ${y}$, we wish to condition on to both the generator and discriminator.

verdict.reasoning: The gap's core problem — the vanilla minimax generator loss log(1-D(G(z))) saturating early when a confident discriminator rejects a weak generator's samples, and the fix of maximizing log D(G(z)) (the non-saturating loss) — is directly addressed by the subsequent literature. MonoFlow gives a mechanistic diagnosis of exactly this failure: it models generator losses as increasing functions of the discriminator's log-density-ratio output and shows why vanilla/MLE losses are flat when the log ratio is very negative (confident D, weak G), while the non-saturated "maximize log σ(d)" objective avoids gradient vanishing because its derivative stays non-negligible for d < 0; it then generalizes this into a loss-design criterion and validates it empirically. LSGAN papers independently address the same saturation/vanishing-gradient failure by substituting a least-squares objective, with theoretical (Pearson χ²) and empirical support, and GAN-QP offers a partial alternative diagnosis around disjoint supports. The exact "maximize log D(G(z))" trick is explained and confirmed rather than newly introduced, and no paper provides formal gradient-norm lower bounds, so the confidence is not maximal; but the specific saturation problem and its non-saturating remedy are squarely diagnosed, validated, and extended.

paper.title: Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss function for the discriminator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stable during the learning process. We evaluate LSGANs on five scene datasets and the experimental results show that the images generated by LSGANs are of better quality than the ones generated by regular GANs. We also conduct two comparison experiments between LSGANs and regular GANs to illustrate the stability of LSGANs.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper identifies exactly the same underlying failure of the original GAN objective: the sigmoid cross-entropy loss used by regular GANs "will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator," and its loss "will saturate when x is relatively large." Its proposed remedy — replacing the sigmoid cross-entropy discriminator loss with a least-squares (quadratic) loss — is designed so that the generator receives non-vanishing gradients (the quadratic loss "is flat only at one point"), which the paper supports with stability experiments and an f-divergence (Pearson χ²) analysis. This directly addresses the general phenomenon of insufficient generator gradients caused by a saturating loss.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific solution is the canonical non-saturating generator objective — "the authors instead maximize log D(G(z))" (replacing min log(1−D(G(z)))) within the original cross-entropy framework — and the gap's canonical failure regime is early training when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples. LSGAN does not implement that fix: it never maximizes log D(G(z)) but instead discards the cross-entropy loss altogether in favor of a least-squares objective, and its motivating failure scenario is somewhat different (fake samples lying correctly classified but far from the decision boundary). Thus, while it solves the broader problem of generator-loss saturation / vanishing gradients, it does so through a different loss mechanism rather than the specific non-saturating-log-D reformulation named in the gap, and it does not evaluate the early-training "confident discriminator rejects G(z)" regime in isolation.
evidence_snippets: Regular GANs adopt the sigmoid cross entropy loss function for the discriminator~[CITE:Goodfellow2014]. We argue that this loss function, however, will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator using the fake samples that are on the correct side of the decision boundary, but are still far from the real data.
Second, penalizing the samples lying a long way to the decision boundary can generate more gradients when updating the generator, which in turn relieves the problem of vanishing gradients.

This benefit can also be derived from another perspective: as shown in Figure [REF:fig:loss], the least squares loss function is flat only at one point, while the sigmoid cross entropy loss function will saturate when $x$ is relatively large.

paper.title: On the Effectiveness of Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven to be hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss for both the discriminator and the generator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. We also show that the derived objective function that yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence performs better than the classical one of using least squares for classification. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stably during the learning process. For evaluating the image quality, we conduct both qualitative and quantitative experiments, and the experimental results show that LSGANs can generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Furthermore, we evaluate the stability of LSGANs in two groups. One is to compare between LSGANs and regular GANs without gradient penalty. We conduct three experiments, including Gaussian mixture distribution, difficult architectures, and a newly proposed method --- datasets with small variability, to illustrate the stability of LSGANs. The other one is to compare between LSGANs with gradient penalty (LSGANs-GP) and WGANs with gradient penalty (WGANs-GP). The experimental results show that LSGANs-GP succeed in training for all the difficult architectures used in WGANs-GP, including 101-layer ResNet.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly tackles the gap's underlying problem — the generator loss saturating/vanishing early in training — and proposes an alternative objective to fix it. It notes that the original paper pointed out M-GANs (minimax loss log(1-D(G(z)))) saturates at the early stage, and argues that both the minimax and non-saturating losses cause vanishing gradients for some fake samples; it proposes Least Squares GANs (LSGANs), whose least-squares generator loss penalizes confidently-rejected samples and stays flat at only one point, thereby providing sustained gradients for G. The paper supports this with theoretical analysis (minimizing the LSGAN objective minimizes the Pearson chi^2 divergence, with no zero-forcing/mode-seeking property) and with extensive qualitative (image quality) and quantitative (FID) plus stability experiments showing LSGANs outperform NS-GANs and are more stable.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper solves the saturation problem with its own loss (least squares) rather than the specific remedy referenced in the gap (maximizing log D(G(z))); in fact it argues that non-saturating log-D still vanishes for fake samples that land on the real-data side of the decision boundary. Its non-saturation argument is largely geometric/heuristic — the formal theory establishes the chi^2-divergence connection and reduced mode-seeking, not a rigorous guarantee that generator gradients stay bounded away from zero in the early regime when D is very confident. So, while the gap's core problem (minimax generator loss saturating early, giving insufficient gradient) is directly and substantially addressed, the paper does not analyze or adopt the exact 'maximize log D' fix of the gap description.
evidence_snippets: They have pointed out that M-GANs will saturate at the early stage of the learning process. Thus NS-GANs are recommended for use in practice.
We argue that both the non-saturating loss and the minimax loss, however, will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator.
the least squares loss function is flat only at one point, while NS-GANs will saturate when $x$ is relatively large, and M-GANs will saturate when $x$ is relatively small.

paper.title: GANs beyond divergence minimization
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can be interpreted as an adversarial game between two players, a discriminator D and a generator G, in which D learns to classify real from fake data and G learns to generate realistic data by "fooling" D into thinking that fake data is actually real data. Currently, a dominating view is that G actually learns by minimizing a divergence given that the general objective function is a divergence when D is optimal. However, this view has been challenged due to inconsistencies between theory and practice. In this paper, we discuss of the properties associated with most loss functions for G (e.g., saturating/non-saturating f-GAN, LSGAN, WGAN, etc.). We show that these loss functions are not divergences and do not have the same equilibrium as expected of divergences. This suggests that G does not need to minimize the same objective function as D maximize, nor maximize the objective of D after swapping real data with fake data (non-saturating GAN) but can instead use a wide range of possible loss functions to learn to generate realistic data. We define GANs through two separate and independent D maximization and G minimization steps. We generalize the generator step to four new classes of loss functions, most of which are actual divergences (while traditional G loss functions are not). We test a wide variety of loss functions from these four classes on a synthetic dataset and on CIFAR-10. We observe that most loss functions converge well and provide comparable data generation quality to non-saturating GAN, LSGAN, and WGAN-GP generator loss functions, whether we use divergences or non-divergences. These results suggest that GANs do not conform well to the divergence minimization theory and form a much broader range of models than previously assumed.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper argues that GAN generator losses are generally not divergences (even at optimal D) and that G need not minimize a divergence or mirror D's objective. It proposes four new classes of generator loss functions (DM, LM, EDM, ELM), some provably divergences, and tests them on a synthetic swiss-roll dataset and CIFAR-10. Along the way it contrasts "saturating" log(1-D(G(z))) versus "non-saturating" log D(G(z)) losses in terms of boundedness, but only as background motivation for its divergence-minimization critique; it does not study or solve the early-training saturation of the minimax objective.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that when G is poor early in training a confident D makes log(1-D(G(z))) saturate and yield insufficient gradient for G, with the remedy being to maximize log D(G(z)) — is not addressed by this paper. The paper merely cites the non-saturating trick as known prior work ("[CITE:GAN] showed that ... non-saturating GAN works much better in practice than directly minimizing the objective of D (saturating GAN)") and uses it as a foil. Its analysis concerns whether generator losses are bounded/unbounded and whether they are divergences, not the vanishing-gradient / early-saturation phenomenon; it neither diagnoses when D's confidence causes gradient collapse nor proposes or evaluates fixes for it (log D(G(z)) is already treated as standard practice, and the paper's own contributions are about alternative loss classes and divergence theory). The saturation problem and its resolution therefore remain entirely outside this paper's scope.

paper.title: MonoFlow: Rethinking Divergence GANs via the Perspective of Wasserstein Gradient Flows
paper.abstract: The conventional understanding of adversarial training in generative adversarial networks (GANs) is that the discriminator is trained to estimate a divergence, and the generator learns to minimize this divergence. We argue that despite the fact that many variants of GANs were developed following this paradigm, the current theoretical understanding of GANs and their practical algorithms are inconsistent. In this paper, we leverage Wasserstein gradient flows which characterize the evolution of particles in the sample space, to gain theoretical insights and algorithmic inspiration of GANs. We introduce a unified generative modeling framework - MonoFlow: the particle evolution is rescaled via a monotonically increasing mapping of the log density ratio. Under our framework, adversarial training can be viewed as a procedure first obtaining MonoFlow's vector field via training the discriminator and the generator learns to draw the particle flow defined by the corresponding vector field. We also reveal the fundamental difference between variational divergence minimization and adversarial training. This analysis helps us to identify what types of generator loss functions can lead to the successful training of GANs and suggest that GANs may have more loss designs beyond the literature (e.g., non-saturated loss), as long as they realize MonoFlow. Consistent empirical studies are included to validate the effectiveness of our framework.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly diagnoses the saturation/gradient-vanishing problem of the vanilla minimax generator objective. Viewing GAN generator losses as increasing functions h of the discriminator's log-density-ratio output, it shows why vanilla and MLE losses saturate early (h' ≈ 0 when the log ratio is very negative, i.e., a confident discriminator facing a weak generator), and why the non-saturated loss (maximize log σ(d)) works, because its derivative stays non-negligible for d < 0. It generalizes this to logit and arcsinh losses, formulates a design criterion (any strictly increasing h whose derivative deviates from zero when d < 0), and empirically validates it, including a shifted-sigmoid fix that makes vanilla GAN training work on MNIST and FID comparisons across generator losses.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper gives a mechanistic/analytical explanation of the saturation and a loss-design recipe, with empirical validation, but it does not supply formal guarantees — no gradient-norm lower bounds, convergence rates, or proofs that the proposed alternative losses avoid saturation in general; the evidence for the new losses (logit, arcsinh, shifted sigmoid) is empirical (2D Gaussians, FID tables, MNIST visualizations). It also does not itself introduce the non-saturated fix (which is prior work by Goodfellow et al.); it explains and extends it. If the validator expects a rigorous, guaranteed non-saturating reformulation of the original minimax objective, that formal part remains open.
evidence_snippets: It is known that the vanilla loss and the MLE loss suffer from the gradient vanishing problem in practice [CITE:goodfellow2016nips]. At the initial training steps, the generator is weak which means the associated $p_g$ is far away from $\pd$. If the discriminator is too good, the estimated log ratio can be extremely small, i.e., $d(\rvx) = \log \big[{\pd(\rvx)}/{p_g(\rvx)}\big] \ll 0$ ... the curves of the vanilla loss and the MLE loss are fairly flat when $d(\rvx)\ll0$, which means the derivative $h'(\cdot)$ is nearly zero.
The NS loss, the logit loss and the arcsinh loss avoid gradient vanishing simply because they have non nearly zero derivatives when $d(\rvx)<0$ despite that the NS loss is flat when $d(\rvx)>0$.

MonoFlow can work with any strictly increasing mappings of the log density ratio and this mapping's derivative should deviate from zero when the $d(\rvx) < 0$ to better avoid too small rescaled vector fields (gradient vanishing).

paper.title: GAN-QP: A Novel GAN Framework without Gradient Vanishing and Lipschitz Constraint
paper.abstract: We know SGAN may have a risk of gradient vanishing. A significant improvement is WGAN, with the help of 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator to prevent from gradient vanishing. Is there any GAN having no gradient vanishing and no 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator? We do find one, called GAN-QP. To construct a new framework of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) usually includes three steps: 1. choose a probability divergence; 2. convert it into a dual form; 3. play a min-max game. In this articles, we demonstrate that the first step is not necessary. We can analyse the property of divergence and even construct new divergence in dual space directly. As a reward, we obtain a simpler alternative of WGAN: GAN-QP. We demonstrate that GAN-QP have a better performance than WGAN in theory and practice.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly addresses the underlying problem of generator gradient saturation/vanishing in GAN training. It identifies the saturating SGAN minimax loss log(1-σ(T(x))), notes that the usual remedy is to swap it for a non-saturating surrogate such as -log σ(T(x)) (= log D(G(z))), and then proposes an alternative: a new quadratic-potential divergence (QP-div) whose induced generator loss T(x_r)-T(x_f) stays non-vanishing even when real and fake distributions are essentially disjoint. It shows QP-div gives nonzero gradients for two point-masses and reports competitive FID results versus WGAN variants.

verdicts.title: Modeling all conditionals via shared parameters
verdicts.description: All conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) can be approximately modeled by training a family of conditional models that share parameters, as a stochastic extension of the deterministic MP-DBM.
verdicts.canonical_description: shared-parameter family of conditional models for all conditionals

evidence.anchor: training a family of conditional models that share parameters
evidence.quote: by training a family of conditional models that share parameters.

verdict.reasoning: The verdict is driven by the Posterior Matching paper, which is a direct solution to the gap's core claim. It trains a single posterior network q(z | x_o) with parameters shared across all observed subsets (encoded via masks) that, combined with any VAE decoder, returns approximate conditionals p(x_u | x_o) for arbitrary disjoint observed/unobserved subsets. The paper supplies a theoretical justification (equivalence of the Posterior Matching objective to arbitrary conditional likelihood) and empirical demonstrations on MNIST, UCI data, clustering, and active feature acquisition across several VAE families — squarely delivering a shared-parameter family of conditional models covering all conditionals. Partition Generative Models gives complementary but partial evidence (random two-way splits with shared parameters), while the Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimator addresses only a fixed conditional and is not relevant. The one caveat is that the gap's literal suggested route — a stochastic extension of the deterministic MP-DBM — is not constructed; Posterior Matching instead attaches the shared conditional mechanism to a VAE latent code, inheriting VAE assumptions. This tempers confidence but does not leave the central problem open, since the all-conditionals shared-parameter modeling claim is directly demonstrated.

paper.title: Posterior Matching for Arbitrary Conditioning
paper.abstract: Arbitrary conditioning is an important problem in unsupervised learning, where we seek to model the conditional densities $p(\mathbf{x}_u \mid \mathbf{x}_o)$ that underly some data, for all possible non-intersecting subsets $o, u \subset \{1, \dots , d\}$. However, the vast majority of density estimation only focuses on modeling the joint distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$, in which important conditional dependencies between features are opaque. We propose a simple and general framework, coined Posterior Matching, that enables Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to perform arbitrary conditioning, without modification to the VAE itself. Posterior Matching applies to the numerous existing VAE-based approaches to joint density estimation, thereby circumventing the specialized models required by previous approaches to arbitrary conditioning. We find that Posterior Matching is comparable or superior to current state-of-the-art methods for a variety of tasks with an assortment of VAEs (e.g.~discrete, hierarchical, VaDE).

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Posterior Matching, which trains a single partially observed posterior network q_theta(z | x_o) (with shared parameters across all observed subsets o, encoded via a mask representation) that, combined with any VAE's decoder, yields approximate conditionals p(x_u | x_o) for arbitrary disjoint subsets o and u — i.e., exactly a shared-parameter family of conditional models covering all conditionals. The authors prove a theorem showing their KL-based Posterior Matching objective is equivalent to maximizing the arbitrary conditional likelihood p(x_u | x_o), and empirically validate arbitrary conditional density estimation/imputation on MNIST, UCI tabular data, clustering with partial observation, and active feature acquisition across several VAE families (VQ-VAE, hierarchical VDVAE, VaDE).
assessments.what_remains_open: The central problem of the gap — approximately modeling all conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) with one shared-parameter conditional model — is directly addressed and demonstrated. What remains open is only the gap's literal suggested route: the paper does not construct a stochastic extension of the deterministic MP-DBM; instead it attaches the shared-parameter conditional network to a VAE latent code. Consequently the approach inherits VAE assumptions (fully observed training data, an existing/pretrained VAE, and typically a factorized decoder for easy sampling), and p(x_u | x_o) is delivered as a latent-matching approximation rather than by directly modeling conditionals of a DBM-type joint model.
evidence_snippets: We propose a simple and general framework, coined Posterior Matching, that enables Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to perform arbitrary conditioning, without modification to the VAE itself.
For flexibility and scalability, it is desirable for a single model to provide all such conditionals at inference time.

we can take an existing VAE that only models the joint distribution $p(\x)$ and train an additional model that, when combined with the VAE, is able to assess any likelihood $p(\xu \mid \xo)$ for arbitrary subsets of unobserved features $\xu$ and observed features $\xo$.

paper.title: Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimation
paper.abstract: We introduce a new framework for training deep generative models for high-dimensional conditional density estimation. The Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimator (BCDE) is a variant of the conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that employs layer(s) of stochastic variables as the bottleneck between the input $x$ and target $y$, where both are high-dimensional. Crucially, we propose a new hybrid training method that blends the conditional generative model with a joint generative model. Hybrid blending is the key to effective training of the BCDE, which avoids overfitting and provides a novel mechanism for leveraging unlabeled data. We show that our hybrid training procedure enables models to achieve competitive results in the MNIST quadrant prediction task in the fully-supervised setting, and sets new benchmarks in the semi-supervised regime for MNIST, SVHN, and CelebA.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper introduces the Bottleneck Conditional Density Estimator (BCDE), a CVAE-variant with stochastic bottleneck variables z between input x and target y for a single conditional p(y|x), together with a hybrid training objective that softly ties the BCDE's parameters to those of a sibling Bottleneck Joint Density Estimator (BJDE) so that unlabeled x and y data can regularize conditional training. Its focus is improving one fixed conditional density estimation task (quadrant prediction, one fixed occlusion split at a time) via joint-conditional blending for semi-supervised learning; it does not construct a shared-parameter family of conditional models covering many conditioning subsets.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap asks for a stochastic analogue of the deterministic MP-DBM in which ALL conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) over arbitrary subsets S of the variables are approximately modeled by a family of conditional models that share parameters, so that one network can answer any masking/partition query. The paper does not do this: it trains a separate conditional model for a fixed x/y partition (each quadrant sub-task is a distinct split, and the paper never ties models across different splits), and its parameter sharing is only between that single conditional BCDE and its joint BJDE sibling (plus factored inference for p(z|x), p(z|y), p(z|x,y)). There is no mechanism or experiment for answering p(x_S | x_notS) for many/general S, no shared family indexed by subsets, and no mention of multi-prediction training or MP-DBM. Thus the core "model all conditionals via shared parameters" problem remains unaddressed.

paper.title: Partition Generative Modeling: Masked Modeling Without Masks
paper.abstract: Masked generative models (MGMs) can generate tokens in parallel and in any order, unlike autoregressive models (ARMs), which decode one token at a time, left-to-right. However, MGMs process the full-length sequence at every sampling step, including mask tokens that carry no information. In contrast, ARMs process only the previously generated tokens. We introduce ``Partition Generative Models'' (PGMs), which replace masking with partitioning. Tokens are split into two groups that cannot attend to each other, and the model learns to predict each group conditioned on the other, eliminating mask tokens entirely. Because the groups do not interact, PGMs can process only the clean tokens during sampling, like ARMs, while retaining parallel, any-order generation, like MGMs. On OpenWebText, PGMs achieve $5-5.5\times$ higher throughput than MDLM while producing samples with lower Generative Perplexity. On ImageNet, PGMs reach comparable FID to MaskGIT with a $7.5\times$ throughput improvement. With twice as many steps, the FID improves to 4.56 while remaining $3.9\times$ faster than MGMs. Finally, PGMs remain compatible with existing MGM samplers and distillation methods.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper introduces Partition Generative Models (PGMs), an encoder–decoder architecture (Partition Transformer with group-wise self-attention and a GroupSwap layer) in which each sequence is split into two non-interacting groups and every position is trained to predict the tokens of the opposite group, with a random group assignment per training sample and time step and fully shared parameters. This removes mask tokens while in expectation training, over random two-way splits, a shared-parameter family of complementary conditional distributions p(group0 | group1) and p(group1 | group0); the model is shown to match MDLM/MaskGIT sample quality at much higher inference throughput and to remain compatible with MGM samplers and distillation.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap asks for modeling *all* conditionals p(x_S | x_notS) for arbitrary subsets S via a shared-parameter family, as a stochastic extension of deterministic MP-DBM. PGM only realizes a restricted version: each forward pass models the two conditionals of a random bipartition (S and its exact complement), and the paper neither proves nor evaluates coverage/quality of arbitrary-subset conditionals. It is framed and validated purely as an unconditional generative model for text/images (perplexity, FID, throughput, distillation), not as a tool for querying arbitrary conditionals p(x_S | x_notS). Moreover, during its inference procedure each chunk is predicted conditioned only on the tokens decoded so far (clean set), not on the full complement x_notS, and the decoded group is sampled from factorized marginals; there is no treatment of the MP-DBM relationship or of all-conditionals modeling quality. Thus the gap's central claim is addressed only partially and indirectly.

verdicts.title: Semi-supervised learning from discriminator features
verdicts.description: Features from the discriminator or inference network could improve classifier performance when limited labeled data is available.
verdicts.canonical_description: semi-supervised learning using discriminator or inference network features

evidence.anchor: from the discriminator or inference net could improve
evidence.quote: \item { Semi-supervised learning}: features from the discriminator or inference net could improve performance

verdict.reasoning: The strongest evidence comes from "Good Semi-supervised Learning that Requires a Bad GAN," which directly addresses the discriminator-feature branch of the gap: in the (K+1)-class GAN SSL setup, the discriminator's learned feature representation is shared with the classifier, and the paper provides theory for when those shared features yield correct decision boundaries plus practical objectives that achieve state-of-the-art limited-label classification on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10. This is a direct, concrete solution to "semi-supervised learning using discriminator features." The inference-network branch is only partially covered: AVAE (Paper 1) feeds VAE-learned inference features to a nearest-neighbor classifier and improves over SSL baselines, but it does not exploit discriminator features and does not demonstrate the very-low-label regime; its authors note that lower supervision remains future work. Papers 2 and 5 offer supporting theory/regularization for discriminator-as-classifier GAN-SSL but do not transfer or extract discriminator/inference features for a separate classifier, and Paper 3 is not addressed. Because the discriminator branch is squarely solved with strong results while the inference-network branch is demonstrated only partially, the overall verdict is solved with moderately high confidence.

paper.title: Adversarial Variational Embedding for Robust Semi-supervised Learning
paper.abstract: Semi-supervised learning is sought for leveraging the unlabelled data when labelled data is difficult or expensive to acquire. Deep generative models (e.g., Variational Autoencoder (VAE)) and semisupervised Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently shown promising performance in semi-supervised classification for the excellent discriminative representing ability. However, the latent code learned by the traditional VAE is not exclusive (repeatable) for a specific input sample, which prevents it from excellent classification performance. In particular, the learned latent representation depends on a non-exclusive component which is stochastically sampled from the prior distribution. Moreover, the semi-supervised GAN models generate data from pre-defined distribution (e.g., Gaussian noises) which is independent of the input data distribution and may obstruct the convergence and is difficult to control the distribution of the generated data. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose a novel Adversarial Variational Embedding (AVAE) framework for robust and effective semi-supervised learning to leverage both the advantage of GAN as a high quality generative model and VAE as a posterior distribution learner. The proposed approach first produces an exclusive latent code by the model which we call VAE++, and meanwhile, provides a meaningful prior distribution for the generator of GAN. The proposed approach is evaluated over four different real-world applications and we show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art models, which confirms that the combination of VAE++ and GAN can provide significant improvements in semisupervised classification.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes AVAE, a semi-supervised framework combining a modified VAE ("VAE++") that learns an exclusive latent code z_I directly from the input (i.e., an inference-network-derived feature) with a semi-supervised GAN whose discriminator adversarially constrains the stochastically sampled code z_s to match z_I's distribution. The learned z_I features are then fed to a classifier and evaluated for semi-supervised classification under various supervision rates across four applications, outperforming VAE- and GAN-based SSL baselines. This bears on the gap because it demonstrates that inference-network features, refined by adversarial/discriminator-driven training, improve classifier performance when labels are limited.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem is learning from "discriminator features" as well as inference-network features. This paper only partially covers that: the classifier never uses discriminator-derived features — the discriminator is used purely as an adversarial constraint (real/fake + class labels), and the authors explicitly reject using the discriminator as the classifier and instead use a separate non-parametric nearest-neighbor classifier on z_I. It also does not demonstrate strong performance under truly small label budgets: experiments range from 20% to 100% supervision, and the authors state that lower supervision rates/unsupervised learning remain future work and that the model "still requires adequate labelled training samples." Thus, exploiting the discriminator's own features as the classification representation, and doing so in a very-low-label regime, remains open.
